en: Sutta Nipāta 3.4 Pūraḷāsa (Sundarikabhāradvāja) Sutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans on the bank of the river Sundarikā.
Now at that time, the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja was offering oblations into the fire and attending to the sacred fire on the bank of the river Sundarikā.
Then, having offered the oblations and attended to the sacred fire, the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja rose from his seat and looked all around in the four directions.
“Who indeed might eat this remains of the sacrificial offering?
Then the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja saw the Blessed One sitting not far away at the foot of a certain tree with his head covered;
having seen him, he took the remains of the offering in his left hand and his water-pot in his right hand, and approached the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One uncovered his head at the sound of Sundarika-Bhāradvāja’s footsteps.
Thereupon, the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja thought, “This worthy one is shaven-headed; this worthy one is a shaveling,” and he desired to turn back right there.
Then it occurred to the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja:
“Indeed, there are some brahmins here who are even shaven-headed; what if I were to approach him and ask about his birth?
Then the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Of what birth are you, sir?”
Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja in verses:
“I am not a brahmin, nor am I a prince;
nor indeed am I anyone of the merchant class.”
Having fully understood the lineage of ordinary worldlings,
I wander the world possessing nothing, mindful and wise;
wearing only my outer robe, I live free from grasping.
"With hair shorn and self extinguished,
unattached here among young men,
you ask me, O Brahmin, about my lineage— a question that is not appropriate for me."
“Indeed, sirs, brahmins ask questions of brahmins;
you, sir, are a brahmin together with us brahmins.
“If you say that I am a brahmin, [then...]”
And you speak of one who is not a brahmin;
that very person I ask about the Sāvitrī,
which has three feet and twenty-four syllables.
“On what did the seers, men,
khattiyas, and brahmins depend upon the deities when they performed numerous sacrifices here in this world?”
“I say that for one who has reached the end, who is a master of knowledge at the time of sacrifice, and whose oblation is accepted—
that for him the offering truly succeeds. Indeed, his offering surely succeeds.
(Thus the Brahmin:
"That we should not see such a master of knowledge as you— indeed, it is through not seeing those like you [that we suffer]."
“Another person eats the sacrificial cake.
“Therefore, O Brahmin, since you have a purpose and are seeking that goal, approach and ask.”
“May I find such a wise one who is peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and desireless.
“I am devoted to sacrifice, O Gotama.”
"I do not understand how one desiring to perform a sacrifice should do so;
may your lordship instruct me—
tell me that wherein what is offered succeeds."
“In that case, brahmin, lend an ear; I shall teach you the Dhamma:
Do not ask about birth, but ask about conduct;
for it is from wood that the fire is born.”
Even one born of a low family, if he is a sage,
possessed of fortitude, noble, and restrained by a sense of shame,
is tamed by truth and endowed with self-control.
A brahmin who seeks merit and would perform sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation at the proper time to one who is a master of the Vedas and has lived the holy life.
To those who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, wander unattached,
upright like a well-strung bowstring because of their excellent self-restraint—
one should offer sacrificial food to them at the proper time.
That brahmin who, seeking merit,
should sacrifice to those who are free from passion, whose faculties are well-composed,
and who are like the moon released from the grasp of Rāhu.
At the proper time, a brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the sacrificial oblation to them;
for they wander through the world unattached.
Always having abandoned the sense of "mine" toward virtuous ones,
a brahmin seeking merit who would sacrifice should offer the oblation to them at the proper time.
He who, having abandoned sensual desires, wanders as a conqueror,
who has realized the end of birth and death—
he is fully extinguished, cool like a pool of water.
The Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
Equal toward equals and unequals, and far removed from the uneven,
the Tathāgata possesses infinite wisdom.
Unstained here or hereafter,
the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake;
in whom neither deceit nor pride dwells.
The brahmin who has cast off greed, is without "mine-ness," and free from longing;
who has expelled anger and whose self is fully quenched—
he has abandoned the stain of sorrow.
The Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake—
he who has abandoned the dwelling of the mind and possesses no attachments whatsoever.
Not grasping at anything here or hereafter,
the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
He who is concentrated has crossed over the flood.
He has understood the Dhamma through supreme vision;
with taints destroyed, bearing his final body,
the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
He for whom the taints of existence and harsh words have been shaken off,
gone to their end, and no longer exist—
he is a knower of the Vedas, liberated in every respect.
The Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
He has transcended attachment; for him there are no attachments, as he is not attached among those who are attached to the mind.
Having fully understood suffering along with its field and its site,
the Tathāgata, seeing seclusion, is worthy of the sacrificial cake,
being independent of hope.
Having transcended views regarding what belongs to another,
for whom there are no objects whatsoever—
such a Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
For one who has thoroughly understood all phenomena, both high and low,
they are blown away, gone to their end, and no longer exist; being peaceful,
he is liberated through the destruction of clinging.
The Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
He is the seer of the destruction of birth and the fetters,
who has eradicated the path of passion without remainder.
Pure, stainless, immaculate, and unblemished,
the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
He who does not perceive a self within himself—
Concentrated, upright, and established in self;
he is indeed unshaken, free from harshness, and without doubt—
the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial offering.
He for whom no inner delusions exist,
who possesses knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena,
and who bears his final body—
And having attained unsurpassed, auspicious full enlightenment;
to this extent is there purity for a yakkha—
the Tathāgata is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
“May my offering be a true offering,
since I have obtained such a master of knowledge;
for the Blessed One, as Brahmā himself, shall be my witness.”
“May the Blessed One eat my sacrificial cake.
“Food offered with a song is not to be eaten by me, O Brahmin;
this is not the Dhamma for those who see clearly.”
The Buddhas reject songs sung to them in verse;
for one established in the Dhamma, O Brahmin, this is the proper conduct.
And they do not honor the Great Sage who has attained perfection by any other means.
One whose taints are destroyed and whose remorse is stilled—
serve him with food and drink,
for he is a field for one who seeks merit.
“It would be well, Blessed One, if you would know me thus:
that one who might enjoy an offering from someone like me,
having sought it out at the time of a sacrifice— ”
Having attained your teaching:
"He from whom contentiousness has departed,
whose mind is undisturbed;
And who is completely freed from sensual desires,
whose sloth has been dispelled— him, the guide across the boundaries of existence, [one should honor].
To one skilled regarding birth and death,
a sage perfected in wisdom—
such a one has come to the sacrifice.
Having put away frowns,
pay homage with palms joined;
honor them with food and drink.
“Thus do offerings succeed.
“The Blessed One is a Buddha, worthy of the sacrificial cake,
the unsurpassed field of merit.”
“An offering to the entire world;
what has been given by the Blessed One bears great fruit.
Then the brahmin Sundarika-Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama made the Dhamma clear in many ways.”
"In this very way, the Blessed Gotama has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
I go for refuge to the Blessed Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed Gotama; may I receive full ordination."
Then the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja attained [the fruits of the path]...
he became an arahant.
Thus ends the fourth discourse, the Sundarikabhāradvājasutta.
